# Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences

Dyah Adila Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of
Wisconsin-Madison, WI, USA Correspondence to: <adila@wisc.edu>   
Changho Shin Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of
Wisconsin-Madison, WI, USA    Yijing Zhang Affiliation: Department of
Computer Science, University of Wisconsin-Madison, WI, USA    Frederic
Sala Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of
Wisconsin-Madison, WI, USA

###### Abstract

Aligning pretrained language models (LMs) often requires large-scale
preference data and substantial computational resources. These costs
become even more prohibitive for multi-objective or pluralistic
alignment. Is this truly necessary? Can we perform _efficient_ alignment
using only internal model capabilities, and without additional training?
To answer this question, we propose AlignEZ, a novel approach that
leverages (1) self-generated preference data and (2) representation
editing to achieve cost-effective, efficient alignment. By operating
directly on learned representations, AlignEZ independently targets
different behavioral aspects without the overhead of traditional
alignment methods. Our experiments reveal that this cost-efficient
procedure improves performance across diverse tasks: up to 19.9% on
general alignment and 1.9% on challenging mathematical reasoning tasks,
even when starting from a strong base model. AlignEZ can also align
models to multiple objectives simultaneously, granting fine-grained
control over multiple preference axes. Finally, we show that AlignEZ can
_accelerate_ more expensive alignment procedures—such as DPO—even under
limited availability of ground-truth preference data.

## 1 Introduction

Large language model (LMs) alignment involves the use of complex and
expensive pipelines ([Schulman et al., 2017](#bib.bib40); [Ouyang et
al., 2022](#bib.bib33); [Rafailov et al., 2024](#bib.bib36)).
Traditional alignment approaches rely on two critical components: (1)
collecting human preference data, and (2) modifying pretrained model
weights to better reflect these preferences. Some methods introduce even
greater complexity, such as RLHF, which requires training a separate
reward model on human preferences before using it for PPO-based model
optimization. This challenge is exacerbated by the emerging need to
align models with multiple, potentially competing preferences and
values, as LMs see diverse deployment across different user groups
([Sorensen et al., 2024](#bib.bib41)).

These strategies face serious scalability challenges. Gathering human
preference data is expensive and time-consuming, and as models grow
larger, the computational demands of fine-tuning become increasingly
prohibitive. This scaling bottleneck raises a fundamental question: What
is the most efficient combination of data and algorithmic approaches
that still enables effective alignment?

This work tackles innovations on both these fronts. For data, one
promising avenue is to exploit the capabilities _already found in the
pretrained model weights_, potentially eliminating the need for external
annotation. This direction builds on mounting evidence suggesting that
alignment primarily serves to reveal knowledge and capabilities acquired
during pretraining ([Zhou et al., 2024](#bib.bib52); [Lin et al.,
2023](#bib.bib26)). Recent work has demonstrated that fine-tuning using
signals derived from the model itself can achieve impressive results,
largely or completely bypassing human annotations ([Fränken et al.,
2024](#bib.bib13); [Wang et al., 2022](#bib.bib48); [Sun et al.,
2023](#bib.bib42); [Sun et al., 2024](#bib.bib43)).

![Refer to caption](2406.03642v2/time_sensitive_exp.png)

Figure 1: Training with DPO (blue) in time-constrained scenarios permits
using only a few samples and produces poor alignment even as sample size
increases (x-axis). AlignEZ (pink) achieves alignment gains even with

![Refer to caption](2406.03642v2/alignez_main_diagram.png)

(4) Example outputs from AlignEZ (top) vs. the base model (bottom).

Parallel to the data challenge, the computational resources needed for
fine-tuning have become extensive. To address this challenge, we aim to
eliminate fine-tuning entirely through a form of _representation
editing_ that requires neither gradient computation nor proxy loss
optimization. While existing representation editing techniques show
promise ([Zou et al.,](#bib.bib53) ; [Wu et al., 2024](#bib.bib49); [Li
et al., 2024](#bib.bib22)), they typically assume access to ground-truth
data–an assumption that becomes problematic when working with noisier
model-derived signals ([Bender et al., 2021](#bib.bib3); [Bommasani et
al., 2021](#bib.bib5); [Kenton et al., 2021](#bib.bib19); [Tamkin et
al., 2021](#bib.bib44)). A detailed review of these data and
computational approaches is provided in the related work section in
Appendix
[A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Related Work ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences").

Our work unifies these two highly efficient strategies—synthetic data
generation from the model itself and representation engineering—through
innovations in both aspects. We demonstrate that pretrained LMs can be
aligned with human preferences using only inherent knowledge, without
requiring additional training or fine-tuning. This is particularly
valuable for scenarios demanding rapid, on-the-fly model personalization
at scale, where neither the time nor the resources are available for
collecting large annotated datasets and running RLHF or DPO. Indeed,
with only a few training samples, DPO struggles to achieve meaningful
alignment, while our more cost-effective approach consistently
outperforms them, as illustrated in Figure
[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences").

To realize this vision, we introduce AlignEZ, a novel approach designed
specifically for this setting. Using the pretrained model’s own
generated preference pairs, AlignEZ identifies alignment-relevant
subspaces within the model’s representations. At inference time, AlignEZ
selectively amplifies desired behaviors and suppresses undesired ones by
editing the model’s hidden embeddings.

This cost-effective procedure improves pretrained model alignment by up
to 19.9% across four tasks and four model architectures. While primarily
designed for alignment, our approach shows promise in improving
specialized capabilities as well. As a proof-of-concept for this
direction, we demonstrate that AlignEZ can improve mathematical
reasoning models by up to 1.9%. Beyond single-objective alignment,
AlignEZ effectively handles multiple preference objectives, enabling
fine-grained control over different alignment dimensions and steering
models along three preference axes simultaneously. We also show that
AlignEZ can _accelerate_ more expensive alignment processes such as DPO.
Notably, we find that applying AlignEZ to a DPO model trained on only 1%
of the ground-truth data achieves performance on par with a DPO model
trained on 25%.

Summary of Contributions:

1.  1.  AlignEZ: A cost-effective, easily deployable approach that uses the
        model’s own self-generated preference data to edit hidden
        representations for alignment.
2.  2.  Substantial Alignment Gains: AlignEZ improves model alignment up to
        19.9% across multiple tasks and architectures. Beyond alignment, it
        shows promise in enhancing specialized capabilities, improving
        mathematical reasoning in expert models by 1.9%.
3.  3.  Multi-objective Steering: AlignEZ enables simultaneous control over
        multiple alignment axes.
4.  4.  Acceleration of Costlier Methods: We show how AlignEZ can expedite
        alignment procedures like DPO, boosting performance when only a
        small fraction of ground-truth preference data is available.

## 2 AlignEZ: Cost-effective LM Alignment

We are ready to describe the AlignEZ algorithm. First, we query a base
pretrained LM to generate its own preference data. Our intuition is
that, while noisy, base models have learned sufficient signal from
pretraining data to permit alignment. Using this self-generated data, we
identify the subspaces in the LM’s embedding spaces that correspond to
directions that aid alignment. During inference, we modify the LM
embeddings using these identified subspaces, steering the model to
generate outputs that better align with human preferences (Figure
[2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences")).

First, we describe the self-generated preference data extraction
procedure in Section
[2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Self-generated Preference Data ‣ 2 AlignEZ: Cost-effective LM Alignment ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences").
Next, we explain alignment subspace identification in Section
[2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Identifying Alignment Subspace ‣ 2 AlignEZ: Cost-effective LM Alignment ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences").
Finally, we detail the embedding editing operation in Section
[2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 Alignment via Embedding Editing ‣ 2 AlignEZ: Cost-effective LM Alignment ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences")
and a layer selection procedure for intervention in Section
[2.4](#S2.SS4 "2.4 Selecting Layers for Intervention. ‣ 2 AlignEZ: Cost-effective LM Alignment ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences").

### 2.1 Self-generated Preference Data

We begin by extracting a human preference signal from the base LLM by
having it generate its own preference data. Our goal is to generate
_diverse_ samples to capture a wide range of alignment signals. For each
query $`q_{i}`$ in dataset $`D`$ of size $`N`$, we prompt the base LM
$`\omega`$ to describe traits for two contrasting agents: a _helpful
agent_ ($`c_{i}^{help}`$) and a _harmful agent_ ($`c_{i}^{harm}`$). For
example, $`c_{i}^{help}`$ might emphasize clarity and relevance, while
$`c_{i}^{harm}`$ highlights vagueness and misleading content.

Next, we create paired prompts by combining each query $`q_{i}`$ with
their corresponding generated characteristics: $`(c_{i}^{help},q_{i})`$
and $`(c_{i}^{harm},q_{i})`$. The model then generates responses for
these paired prompts, producing preference pairs
$`(p_{i}^{help},p_{i}^{harm})`$. These pairs form two distinct datasets
$`P^{help}`$ and $`P^{harm}`$, as illustrated in Figure
[2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences").

We use fixed prompt templates with minimal task-specific adjustments.
For instance, in writing tasks, we adapt the prompts to contrast a
“creative agent” with a “dull and boring agent”. Complete examples of
generated samples and prompts are provided in Appendix
[A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Prompt Template ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences")
and
[B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Analysis on Self-Generated Characteristics (Warning: Some text might be considered disturbing) ‣ Appendix B Additional analysis ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences"),
respectively.

Since the base LLM is neither aligned nor instruction-tuned, some
responses may deviate from the intended characteristics. To mitigate
this noise, we filter out pairs that are too similar in the LLM’s
embedding space, a technique shown to reduce the likelihood of
dispreferred responses ([Razin et al., 2024](#bib.bib38)). This
filtering helps maintain a more accurate and _diverse_ set of
alignment-relevant examples.

### 2.2 Identifying Alignment Subspace

Next, we identify the human preference subspace in the embedding space
of the model using self-generated preference pairs. Adapting methods
from word embedding debiasing ([Bolukbasi et al., 2016](#bib.bib4)), we
apply singular value decomposition (SVD) to the differences between
preferred and dispreferred response embeddings to extract the subspace
that capture alignment. We take the MLP output activation values at each
layer’s final token position as our embeddings.

Concretely, let $`\Phi_{l}`$ denote the function mapping an input
sentence to the embedding space at layer $`l`$. For each preference pair
$`(p_{i}^{help},p_{i}^{harm})`$, we compute the corresponding embeddings
$`\Phi_{l}(p_{i}^{help})`$ and $`\Phi_{l}(p_{i}^{harm})`$. Next, we
construct embedding matrices for helpful and harmful preferences:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\textbf{H}_{l}^{help}:=\begin{bmatrix}\Phi_{l}(p_{1}^{help})\\
\vdots\\
\Phi_{l}(p_{K}^{help})\end{bmatrix}^{T},\quad\textbf{H}_{l}^{harm}:=\begin{bmatrix}\Phi_{l}(p_{1}^{harm})\\
\vdots\\
\Phi_{l}(p_{K}^{harm})\end{bmatrix}^{T},
``` |  |

where $`K`$ is the total number of preference pairs.

The alignment subspace is identified by computing the difference between
the helpful and harmful embeddings:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\textbf{H}_{l}^{align}:=\textbf{H}_{l}^{help}-\textbf{H}_{l}^{harm}.
``` |  | (1) |

We then perform SVD on $`\textbf{H}_{l}^{align}`$:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle`$ | $`\displaystyle\textbf{H}_{l}^{align}=\textbf{U}\Sigma\textbf{V}`$ |  | (2) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\Theta_{l}^{align}:=\textbf{V}^{T},`$ |  |  |

where U and V are the left and right unitary matrices, respectively, and
$`\Sigma`$ is the diagonal matrix of singular values. The columns of V
define our alignment subspace $`\Theta_{l}^{align}`$.

##### Sample-conditional estimation of $`\Theta_{l}^{align}`$.

To prevent certain directions from dominating the intervention, we
filter which directions in the alignment subspace $`\Theta_{l}^{align}`$
are applied to *each test query*. We define two subsets of
$`\Theta_{l}^{align}`$ for a query $`q`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Theta_{l,help}^{align}(q):=\left\{\,\theta\in\Theta_{l}^{align}\,\middle|\,\cos\left(\Phi_{l}(q),\theta\right)\leq 0\right\},
``` |  |

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Theta_{l,harm}^{align}(q):=\left\{\,\theta\in\Theta_{l}^{align}\,\middle|\,\cos\left(\Phi_{l}(q),\theta\right)>0\right\}.
``` |  |

Our use of these subspaces is task-dependent. For tasks prioritizing the
addition of helpful information, we set
$`\Theta_{l}^{align}:=\Theta_{l,help}^{align}(q)`$, which contains
directions orthogonal or opposed to the query’s embedding. Conversely,
for tasks focused on reducing harmful content (e.g., jailbreaking
prevention), we use $`\Theta_{l}^{align}:=\Theta_{l,harm}^{align}(q)`$,
which contains directions aligned with the query’s embedding. This
ensures that only directions that do not already align with the query’s
embedding (for addition) or directions that do strongly overlap with it
are considered, preventing any single direction from dominating the
intervention.

### 2.3 Alignment via Embedding Editing

Using the identified alignment subspace $`\Theta_{l}^{align}`$, we
modify the model’s embeddings during inference. Let $`x_{l}`$ be the MLP
output at layer $`l`$. The editing process is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\hat{x}_{l}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leftarrow x_{l},`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\text{for each }\theta_{l}\in\Theta_{l}^{align}:\quad\hat{x}_{l}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leftarrow\hat{x}_{l}+\alpha\,\sigma\!\bigl(\langle\hat{x}_{l},\theta_{l}\rangle\bigr)\,\theta_{l},`$ |  |

where $`\sigma(\cdot)`$ is an activation function and
$`\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle`$ denotes inner product. We iteratively
adjust $`\hat{x}_{l}`$ by moving it toward or away from each direction
$`\theta_{l}`$ in $`\Theta_{l}`$. For harmful subspace removal, we set
$`\sigma(\cdot)=\mathrm{ReLU}(\cdot)`$ with $`\alpha=-1`$, ensuring
subtraction only when $`\hat{x}_{l}`$ aligns with harmful directions.
For helpful subspaces, we set $`\sigma(\cdot)=\tanh(\cdot)`$ with
$`\alpha=1`$, enabling smooth bidirectional scaling bounded by
$`[-1,1]`$.

### 2.4 Selecting Layers for Intervention.

The last piece of the puzzle is choosing which layers to edit.
Intuitively, we focus on layers $`l`$ where the alignment between
$`\Theta_{l}^{align}`$ and query embeddings is strongest, as these
capture more of the helpful or harmful content we aim to modify. For
each layer $`l`$, we compute:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
s_{l}=\left\|\sum_{\theta_{l}\in\Theta_{l}^{align}}\langle\Phi_{l}^{q},\theta_{l}\rangle\theta_{l}\right\|.
``` |  |

We select the top-$`k`$ layers with highest $`s_{l}`$ scores, targeting
our modifications where they will be most effective.

## 3 Theoretical Analysis

We provide a formal analysis to characterize the conditions under which
AlignEZ can enhance alignment. Let $`{\mathcal{V}}`$ denote a
vocabulary, and $`{\mathcal{V}}^{*}`$ be the set sequences over it.
Define a query $`q\in{\mathcal{V}}`$ with its hidden embedding
represented as $`h_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}`$. Additionally, let
$`U\in\mathbb{R}^{|{\mathcal{V}}|\times k}`$ be the token unembedding
matrix. For an output sequence $`y\in{\mathcal{V}}^{*}`$, the
probability of generating the sequence is expressed as:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{P}(y\mid q)=\prod_{j=1}^{|y|}\mathrm{P}(y_{j}\mid q,y_{<j})=\prod_{j=1}^{|y|}\text{softmax}(Uh_{[q,y_{<j}]}).
``` |  |

We assume a linear representation hypothesis ([Park et al.,
2024](#bib.bib34); [Adila et al., 2023](#bib.bib1)), which posits that
each word representation can be expressed as a linear combination of
latent concepts $`Z=\{z_{1},z_{2},\ldots,z_{k}\}`$. These latent
concepts are orthonormal vectors that form a basis. Consequently, a word
embedding vector $`u_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}`$ can be expressed as
$`u_{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\beta_{i,j}z_{i}`$. Similarly, the hidden
embedding vector $`h_{q}`$ can be written as
$`h_{q}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_{i}z_{i}`$.

Under this framework, the prediction of the next single token is given
by:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{y}=\arg\max_{j}h_{q}^{T}u_{j}=\arg\max_{j}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_{i}\beta_{i,j}.
``` |  |

We partition the latent concepts into three groups:
$`Z^{harm}=\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{S}\}`$,
$`Z^{help}=\{z_{S+1},\ldots,z_{S+R}\}`$,
$`Z^{benign}=\{z_{S+R+1},\ldots,z_{S+R+B}\}`$, representing harmful,
helpful, benign concepts, respectively. These are specific to the
desired type of alignment.

To enhance alignment, our objectives are to reduce
$`\alpha_{i}^{\text{harm}}`$ and increase $`\alpha_{i}^{\text{help}}`$,
thereby selecting better aligned tokens in next token prediction. We
define $`\theta^{\text{harm}}_{L,1},\ldots,\theta^{\text{harm}}_{L,S}`$
and $`\theta^{\text{help}}_{L,1},\ldots,\theta^{\text{help}}_{L,R}`$ as
the harmful and helpful directions, respectively. These directions are
derived from the sample-conditioned estimation of
$`\Theta^{\text{align}}_{L,\text{harm}}`$ and
$`\Theta^{\text{align}}_{L,\text{help}}`$, where $`L`$ denotes the last
layer.

Each alignment vector can also be decomposed into the latent concepts:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\theta_{L,s}^{\text{harm}}=\sum_{i=1}^{S+R+B}\gamma_{i,s}z_{i}\quad\text{for }1\leq s\leq S,
``` |  |

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\theta_{L,r}^{\text{help}}=\sum_{i=1}^{S+R+B}\gamma_{i,r}z_{i}\quad\text{for }S+1\leq r\leq S+R.
``` |  |

We further assume that the benign components of the alignment vectors
constitute Gaussian noise, such that

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\gamma_{i,b}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\sigma_{\text{benign}}^{2}\right)\quad\text{for }S+R+1\leq b\leq S+R+B.
``` |  |

For each $`1\leq i\leq S+R`$, we assume that $`\gamma_{i,i}`$ are
constant values, thereby capturing the $`i`$-th latent concept.
Additionally, we assume that

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\gamma_{i,j}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\sigma_{\text{align}}^{2}\right)\quad\text{for }i\neq j\text{ and }1\leq j\leq S+R,
``` |  |

indicating that non-target alignment axes may be affected by noise.

We simplify the AlignEZ procedure by removing its non-linearity and
considering only the last layer as follows.

##### Removing Harmful Component

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\hat{h}_{q,-}`$ | $`\displaystyle=h_{q}-\sum_{s=1}^{S}\frac{h_{q}^{\top}\theta_{L,s}^{\text{harm}}}{\|\theta_{L,s}^{\text{harm}}\|^{2}}\theta_{L,s}^{\text{harm}}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{S}\alpha_{i,-}^{\text{help}}z_{i}+\sum_{i=S+1}^{S+R}\alpha_{i,-}^{\text{harm}}z_{i}+\sum_{i=S+R+1}^{S+R+B}\alpha_{i,-}^{\text{benign}}z_{i}.`$ |  |

##### Boosting Helpful Component

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\hat{h}_{q,+}`$ | $`\displaystyle=h_{q}+\sum_{r=S+1}^{S+R}\frac{h_{q}^{\top}\theta_{L,r}^{\text{help}}}{\|\theta_{L,r}^{\text{help}}\|^{2}}\theta_{L,r}^{\text{help}}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{S}\alpha_{i,+}^{\text{help}}z_{i}+\sum_{i=S+1}^{S+R}\alpha_{i,+}^{\text{harm}}z_{i}+\sum_{i=S+R+1}^{S+R+B}\alpha_{i,+}^{\text{benign}}z_{i}.`$ |  |

We analyze the coefficients after applying AlignEZ (i.e.,
$`\alpha^{\text{harm}}_{i,-}`$ and $`\alpha^{\text{help}}_{i,+}`$). The
following theorems demonstrate the effect of AlignEZ on the coefficients
of the latent concepts.

###### Theorem 3.1.

Under the noise model described above, the coefficient
$`\alpha^{harm}_{s,-}`$ for the harmful concept $`z_{s}`$ satisfies

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle|\mathbb{E}{\alpha^{harm}_{s,-}}|`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\left|\alpha^{harm}_{s}\left(\cfrac{(S+R-1)\sigma_{align}^{2}+B\sigma_{benign}^{2}}{\gamma_{s,s}^{2}+(S+R-1)\sigma_{align}^{2}+B\sigma_{benign}^{2}}\right)\right|`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle+\left|\sum_{t\neq s}^{S}\cfrac{\alpha_{s}\sigma_{align}^{2}}{\gamma_{t,t}^{2}}\right|.`$ |  |

###### Theorem 3.2.

Under the given noise model, the coefficient $`\alpha^{help}_{r,+}`$ for
the helpful concept $`r`$ satisfies

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}{\alpha^{help}_{r,+}}\geq\left(\cfrac{2\gamma_{r,r}^{2}+(S+B-1)\sigma_{align}^{2}+B\sigma^{2}_{benign}}{\gamma_{r,r}^{2}+(S+B-1)\sigma_{align}^{2}+B\sigma^{2}_{benign}}\right)\alpha_{r}.
``` |  |

Both theorems imply that alignment is enhanced when alignment vectors
have strong signals (i.e., large $`\gamma_{i,i}`$ for
$`1\leq i\leq S+R`$) and when alignment and benign noise are minimal
(i.e., small $`\sigma_{\text{align}}`$ and $`\sigma_{\text{benign}}`$).
Proofs and detailed explanations are provided in Appendix
[C](#A3 "Appendix C Theory details ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences").

## 4 Experiments

We evaluate the following claims about AlignEZ.

- •
  Improving pretrained model alignment (Section
  [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Improving Pretrained Model Alignment ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences")).
  AlignEZ improves the base model alignment capabilities without
  fine-tuning and ground-truth preference data.
- •
  Enabling multi-objective control (Section
  [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Enabling Multi-Objective Control ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences")).
  AlignEZ effectively steers models along multiple preference axes at
  inference time, allowing fine-grained control over the influence of
  each axis.
- •
  Expediting alignment (Section
  [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Expediting Alignment ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences")).
  AlignEZ *expedites DPO alignment* by improving models that have been
  fine-tuned using DPO on *only a small* subset of ground-truth
  preference data.
- •
  Enhancing specialized knowledge (Section
  [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Enhancing Specialized Knowledge ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences")).
  AlignEZ demonstrates potential in improving specialized knowledge,
  showing gains on challenging multi-hop mathematical reasoning task.

### 4.1 Improving Pretrained Model Alignment

First, we assess how effectively AlignEZ improves the performance of the
base pretrained model.

##### Setup.

All experiments use frozen LLM weights, with no additional training. We
arbitrarily set the number of layers to edit to 5 across all
experiments.

##### Metrics.

We follow standard automatic alignment evaluation, using GPT-4 as a
judge to compare pairs of model responses ([Zheng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib51)). For each comparison, we calculate the win rate (W%)
– the proportion of responses judged better than the pretrained model;
and lose rate (L%)– the proportion judged worse. We define net
improvement as Net Win% ($`\Delta\%`$) $`=`$ W% $`-`$ L%. A positive
$`\Delta\%`$ indicates that the model more frequently produces improved
responses compared to the pretrained model.

##### Datasets.

To evaluate the generalization capability of AlignEZ in various tasks
while keeping the evaluation affordable, we use just-eval-instruct
dataset ([Lin et al., 2023](#bib.bib26)). This dataset is a diverse
collection of queries created by sampling and merging several datasets,
namely AlpacaEval ([Li et al., 2023b](#bib.bib24)), MT-Bench ([Zheng et
al., 2024](#bib.bib51)), and LIMA ([Zhou et al., 2024](#bib.bib52)). We
split the dataset based on the provided task label and evaluate AlignEZ
on three tasks: (1) Math + Coding, (2) Commonsense reasoning, (3)
Writing. Additionally, we evaluate AlignEZ on the safeguarding task in
red-teaming scenarios using the JailBreakBench ([Chao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib6)).

##### Baseline.

We compare AlignEZ to several pretrained models of different sizes:
Llama 3.2-1B, Llama 3.2-3B, Llama 3.1-8B ([Touvron et al.,
2023](#bib.bib45)), and Mistral-Nemo-Base-2407 (12B) ([Jiang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib18)). We also compare AlignEZ against test-time alignment
methods, such as Activation Steering. Specifically, we implement the CAA
([Rimsky et al., 2023](#bib.bib39)) and ITI ([Li et al.,
2024](#bib.bib22)) methods, using ground-truth preference data from the
hh-rlhf ([Bai et al., 2022](#bib.bib2); [Ganguli et al.,
2022](#bib.bib14)) dataset to compute the steering vector (the vector
used to adjust the model’s activations). For each experiment, we sample
300 random examples. The optimal intervention layer for CAA and ITI
hyperparameters are selected based on validation using the MT-Bench
slice of just-eval-instruct.

##### Results.

Table
[1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Boosting Helpful Component ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences")
shows that across various tasks and model architectures, AlignEZ
delivers consistent improvements, achieving positive gains in 87.5% of
cases with an average $`\Delta\%`$ of 7.2%. Notably, AlignEZ shows more
reliable performance than the test-time alignment baselines, with ITI
and CAA achieving positive improvements in only 75% and 56.3% of cases.
Most importantly, AlignEZ achieves these results *without* requiring
ground-truth preference data (unlike ITI and CAA), underscoring its
effectiveness in real-world scenarios where such data may be limited.

### 4.2 Enabling Multi-Objective Control

We now evaluate AlignEZ’s capability for multi-objective control through
two experimental scenarios: (1) Modulating paired output characteristics
with varying weights (Figure
[3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Boosting Helpful Component ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences")),
and (2) Simultaneously improving three distinct preference axes (Figure
[4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Boosting Helpful Component ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences")).

##### Setup.

We evaluate on a Llama 3.2-3B model and follow the setup from [Yang et
al. (2024)](#bib.bib50), using three preference axes: *helpfulness*,
*harmlessness*, and *humor*. Our evaluation uses 300 randomly sampled
prompts from the hh-rlhf dataset. In the first experiment, we modulate
the steering between two preference axes by applying weight pairs
$`(\alpha,1-\alpha)`$, where $`\alpha`$ ranges from 0.1 to 0.9 in
increments of 0.1. In the second experiment, we apply AlignEZ using the
combined subspace
$`\Theta^{align}=\Theta^{align}_{\cdot,helpful}\cup\Theta^{align}_{\cdot,harmless}\cup\Theta^{align}_{\cdot,humor}`$.
Both experiments use the base model (Vanilla) as a baseline, and the
second experiment additionally compares against an RLHF-tuned model
(Instruct). All baseline models are prompted to generate outputs
corresponding to the target preferences. Complete prompt details are
provided in Appendix
[A.3.3](#A1.SS3.SSS3 "A.3.3 Multi-objective experiment prompts ‣ A.3 Prompt Template ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences").

##### Metrics.

We measure the performance on each preference axis (helpful, harmless,
humor) using open-source reward models from HuggingFace, then compute
the average reward score for each axis. Further details on the reward
models is in Appendix
[B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Reward Model Details ‣ Appendix B Additional analysis ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences").

##### Results.

Figure
[3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Boosting Helpful Component ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences")
demonstrates AlignEZ’s precise control over paired preferences. The
model effectively modulates outputs between (helpfulness, humor) and
(harmlessness, humor), with reward scores closely tracking the assigned
steering weights. However, steering between helpfulness and harmlessness
shows limited effect due to their inherent correlation, as confirmed by
the cosine similarities shown in the figure.

Beyond pairwise control, Figure
[4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Boosting Helpful Component ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences")
shows that AlignEZ can successfully optimize all three preferences
simultaneously, achieving performance that surpasses even an RLHF-tuned
model specifically prompted for these characteristics. Detailed prompts
are provided in Appendix
[A.3.3](#A1.SS3.SSS3 "A.3.3 Multi-objective experiment prompts ‣ A.3 Prompt Template ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences").

![Refer to caption](2406.03642v2/figs/DPO.png)

Figure 5: DPO with 1% data + AlignEZ matches the performance of DPO with
25% data (blue dashed line).

### 4.3 Expediting Alignment

This experiment evaluates AlignEZ’s ability to expedite more expensive
alignment techniques like DPO. We test whether AlignEZ can improve
models trained with DPO using only a smaller subset of ground-truth
preference data.

##### Setup.

We perform DPO fine-tuning on the Mistral-7b-base model using the
UltraFeedback-binarized dataset ([Cui et al., 2023](#bib.bib10);
[Tunstall et al., 2023](#bib.bib46)) and do evaluation on the test set.
We measure Net Win ($`\Delta\%`$) using GPT-4 as a judge against the
base model. We provide the complete DPO training parameters in the
Appendix
[C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 DPO Training details ‣ Appendix C Theory details ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences").

##### Results.

Figure
[5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Results. ‣ 4.2 Enabling Multi-Objective Control ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences")
shows that AlignEZ significantly improves the alignment of models
trained with DPO using a small subset of ground-truth preference data.
Remarkably, it boosts the performance of DPO with just 1% of the data to
match that achieved with 25%. This confirms that AlignEZ can effectively
accelerate traditional alignment approaches, offering substantial gains
when ground-truth preference data is limited.

| Model              | Dataset | Method  | pass@1 |
|--------------------|---------|---------|--------|
| DeepSeek-R1 (1.5B) | SVAMP   | Vanilla | 81.8   |
|                    |         | AlignEZ | 82.5   |
|                    | AQuA    | Vanilla | 53.6   |
|                    |         | AlignEZ | 54.4   |
| DeepSeek-R1 (7B)   | SVAMP   | Vanilla | 89.0   |
|                    |         | AlignEZ | 89.6   |
|                    | AQuA    | Vanilla | 55.7   |
|                    |         | AlignEZ | 57.6   |

Table 2: AlignEZ improves multi-hop math reasoning

### 4.4 Enhancing Specialized Knowledge

Beyond alignment, we explore AlignEZ’s potential to enhance specialized
capabilities by applying it to challenging multi-hop mathematical
reasoning tasks.

##### Setup.

We evaluate on the DeepSeek-R1 model using two multi-step arithmetic
reasoning benchmarks: SVAMP ([Patel et al., 2021](#bib.bib35)) and AQuA
([Ling et al., 2017](#bib.bib27)). Following standard practice for
long-form reasoning evaluation, we use the Pass@1 metric ([Chen et al.,
2021](#bib.bib7)). For this experiment, we adapt our preference
generation approach: instead of using helpful and harmful
characteristics, we generate $`P^{help}`$ by requesting *more
step-by-step reasoning* and $`P^{harm}`$ by instructing the model to
*provide direct answers without reasoning steps*.

##### Results.

Table
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Results. ‣ 4.3 Expediting Alignment ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences")
shows that AlignEZ improves performance by 0.6%-1.9% across these
benchmarks. We attribute these gains to the identified
$`\Theta^{align}`$ subspace, which appears to strengthen the model’s
tendency toward step-by-step reasoning while suppressing shortcuts to
direct answers.

| Model          | Task          | $`P^{help}`$ | $`P^{harm}`$ | Win% |
|----------------|---------------|--------------|--------------|------|
| Llama-3.2 (1B) | Math + Coding | 0.38         | 0.32         | 69.9 |
|                | Reasoning     | 0.58         | 0.50         | 59.9 |
|                | Writing       | 0.42         | 0.40         | 56.2 |
|                | Red-teaming   | 0.30         | 0.27         | 55.8 |
| Llama-3.1 (8B) | Math + Coding | 0.58         | 0.46         | 62.0 |
|                | Reasoning     | 0.84         | 0.65         | 58.8 |
|                | Writing       | 0.73         | 0.54         | 63.0 |
|                | Red-teaming   | 0.40         | 0.24         | 71.8 |

Table 3: Normalized reward of generated preference pairs. While somewhat
noisy, they demonstrate the intended property: helpful samples
consistently have higher reward than harmful ones.

## 5 Synthetic Data Analysis

We analyze the properties of AlignEZ’s generated synthetic data to
understand how it boosts alignment.

### 5.1 Does the pre-trained model generated data have the intended properties?

We evaluate the quality of synthetic preference pairs generated by the
base pretrained models from the perspective of the difference between
$`P^{\text{help}}`$ and $`P^{\text{harm}}`$. This distinction is crucial
because it directly impacts the embedding difference calculated in
Equation
[1](#S2.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ 2.2 Identifying Alignment Subspace ‣ 2 AlignEZ: Cost-effective LM Alignment ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences")
and, consequently, the alignment subspace identified in Equation
[2](#S2.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ 2.2 Identifying Alignment Subspace ‣ 2 AlignEZ: Cost-effective LM Alignment ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences").
If the distributions are insufficiently different, the resulting
embedding difference would be too small to yield an effective alignment
direction.

##### Setup.

To evaluate the quality of our synthetic data, we employ the Skywork
Reward Model ([Liu et al., 2024](#bib.bib28)), which has been trained on
diverse preference pairs spanning multiple domains (mathematics, coding,
writing, commonsense reasoning, and harmlessness for red-teaming). We
measure the average normalized rewards for both helpful ($`P^{help}`$)
and harmful ($`P^{harm}`$) samples. We also compute the win rate (Win%),
defined as the proportion of cases where a helpful sample
($`p_{i}^{help}`$) obtains a higher reward than its corresponding
harmful sample ($`p_{i}^{harm}`$).

##### Result.

Table
[3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Results. ‣ 4.4 Enhancing Specialized Knowledge ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences")
demonstrates a clear distinction between the average rewards of
$`P^{\text{help}}`$ and $`P^{\text{harm}}`$ samples. This separation is
robust across model scales, notably persisting even in smaller models
like the Llama 3.2 series. The distinction is further supported by
consistent Win rates exceeding 55% across all configurations. These
findings strongly validate the effectiveness of our synthetic preference
pairs: $`P^{\text{help}}`$ samples reliably exhibit task-relevant
helpful behaviors, while $`P^{\text{harm}}`$ samples systematically lack
these desired properties. For comprehensive results see Appendix
[B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Synthetic Data Quality full table ‣ Appendix B Additional analysis ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences").

### 5.2 On the diminishing return of self-generated data

Our previous analysis reveals promising alignment properties in
model-generated preference data. This raises a natural question: Why not
generate such data at scale for traditional gradient-based methods? To
investigate this, we examine two aspects of synthetic data: quality and
diversity. High-quality, diverse samples are essential for capturing
broad alignment signals, while low diversity suggests redundancy that
provides diminishing returns.

##### Setup.

We quantify data diversity by computing the average pairwise distance
between samples in the embedding space using sentence embedding model.

##### Result.

Figure
[6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Results. ‣ 4.4 Enhancing Specialized Knowledge ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences")
reveals a significant decline in quality and diversity as the number of
generated samples increases. Interestingly, the general reward for
helpful samples decreases, and the distinction between helpful and
harmful samples becomes less pronounced. These findings indicate that
scaling up synthetic data generation for data-hungry methods like DPO is
likely counterproductive. This limitation of synthetic data scaling
underscores the need for more efficient approaches that can effectively
leverage smaller quantities of synthetic data—precisely the challenge
our representation editing method addresses.

## 6 Conclusion

We present AlignEZ, a cost-efficient approach that achieves model
alignment by leveraging inherent model knowledge through self-generated
preference data and representation editing. Our experiments demonstrate
that AlignEZ significantly improves model performance across diverse
tasks and architectures without additional training and ground-truth
preference data. Beyond single-objective alignment, AlignEZ enables
precise control over multiple alignment axes simultaneously. The method
also shows promise beyond its primary focus on alignment, demonstrating
potential in enhancing specialized capabilities, as shown by
improvements in challenging mathematical reasoning. These results
suggest broader applications for AlignEZ and future methods that build
upon it for adding new model capabilities and advanced reasoning.

## Appendix A Appendix

### A.1 Related Work

Our work tackles alignment and sits at the intersection of
self-generated synthetic data and efficient model editing. We give a
(necessarily) compressed introduction to these areas.

##### LM Alignment.

The standard approach to aligning LMs with human values and preferences
relies on human-annotated preference data. This data is used either to
(i) train a reward function and subsequently fine-tune the LM to
maximize this reward using reinforcement learning objectives, as in
methods like RLHF ([Ouyang et al., 2022](#bib.bib33); [Christiano et
al., 2017](#bib.bib8)), or (ii) optimize a proxy loss to maximize the
margin between preferred and not preferred outputs, as in methods like
DPO ([Rafailov et al., 2024](#bib.bib36)). While these methods achieve
remarkable performance, they are challenging to implement due to their
complex pipelines, the high cost of computing resources, and the limited
scalability of acquiring human-preference data.

Meanwhile, [Sorensen et al. (2024)](#bib.bib41) propose a framework for
pluralistic alignment that respects diverse human values and preferences
in AI systems. They argue that successful pluralistic alignment requires
both theoretical advances in multi-objective optimization and practical
implementations that can handle conflicting values while maintaining
robustness. Our method facilitates pluralistic alignment through
inference-time adaptation using self-generated synthetic data and
representation editing.

##### Self-Improvement.

The difficulty of obtaining human-annotated data has led to significant
efforts to bypass this requirement. Methods such as those proposed by
[Wang et al. (2022)](#bib.bib48); [Sun et al. (2024)](#bib.bib43);
[McIntosh et al. (2023)](#bib.bib31) use manually crafted seed prompts
to generate high-quality synthetic datasets from pretrained LMs, which
are then used for fine-tuning or training reward models. [Guo et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib15) uses retrieval-augmented generation to remove
reliance on manually designed prompts. Another approach, [Li et al.
(2023a)](#bib.bib23), leverages instruction-tuned models to assist in
generating synthetic datasets. The work most similar to our approach is
[Fränken et al. (2024)](#bib.bib13), which emphasizes maximizing the use
of knowledge from the pretrained model being aligned. [Huang et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib17) introduces the sharpening mechanism, where language
models refine their outputs through self-evaluation. They analyze this
process under SFT and RLHF, showing that RLHF can outperform SFT by
leveraging exploration. Our work takes this further by exploring whether
self-alignment can be made even more cost-effective by replacing
fine-tuning with representation editing, dramatically accelerating the
alignment process.

##### Representation Editing.

A parallel line of work seeks to modify model behavior without
fine-tuning—doing so by solely editing the model’s representations. For
vision-language models like CLIP, [Adila et al. (2023)](#bib.bib1) and
[Chuang et al. (2023)](#bib.bib9) show that removing spurious or
unwanted concept subspaces from embeddings boosts model accuracy on rare
class predictions. [Limisiewicz et al. (2023)](#bib.bib25) shows that
doing so in LLM architectures reduces gender bias in generated sentences
without degrading model performance in other tasks. [Zou et al.
()](#bib.bib53); [Li et al. (2024)](#bib.bib22); [Han et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib16); [Rimsky et al. (2023)](#bib.bib39) demonstrate that
modifying embeddings during inference to steer them towards certain
traits (e.g., honesty, truthfulness, sentiment) can effectively enhance
these traits in the generated outputs. Similarly, [Wu et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib49) and [Kong et al. (2024)](#bib.bib21) learn the
appropriate embedding modification, acting as a form of fine-tuning.
[Uppaal et al. (2024)](#bib.bib47) establishes a connection between DPO
and model editing, demonstrating that model editing effectively reduces
toxicity when provided with accurate preference pairs. *These methods
assume access to ground-truth preference datasets*. Our work
differentiates itself by designing an intervention technique that can
handle the noisier signal from synthetic data generated by LMs.

### A.2 Glossary

Table
[4](#A1.T4 "Table 4 ‣ A.2 Glossary ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences")
shows glossary of terms used in this paper.

| Symbol | Definition |
|----|----|
| $`D`$ | Dataset of queries |
| $`q_{i}`$ | Sample query |
| $`\omega`$ | Language Model |
| $`l`$ | Language model layer index |
| $`c_{i}^{help}`$ | Characteristic of helpful answer |
| $`c_{i}^{help}`$ | Characteristic of harmful/unhelpful answer |
| $`p_{i}^{help}`$ | Helpful preference sample |
| $`P^{help}`$ | Self generated helpful preference data |
| $`P^{harm}`$ | Self generated harmful/unpreferred preference data |
| $`\Theta^{align}`$ | Alignment subspace |
| $`\Phi_{l}`$ | Function that maps an input sentence to the embedding space at layer $`l`$. |
| $`\Phi_{i,l}^{help}`$ | Embedding of $`p_{i}^{help}`$ in layer $`l`$ of $`\omega`$, abbreviation of $`\Phi_{l}(p_{i}^{help})`$ |
| $`\Phi_{i,l}^{harm}`$ | Embedding of $`p_{i}^{harm}`$ in layer $`l`$ of $`\omega`$, abbreviation of $`\Phi_{l}(p_{i}^{harm})`$ |
| $`\textbf{H}_{l}^{help}`$ | Embedding matrix stacked from $`\Phi_{i,l}^{help}`$ |
| $`\textbf{H}_{l}^{harm}`$ | Embedding matrix stacked from $`\Phi_{i,l}^{harm}`$ |
| $`x_{l}`$ | Output of MLP at layer $`l`$ |
| $`\hat{x_{l}}`$ | MLP output after AlignEZ embedding edit |
| $`h_{q}`$ | Query embedding, abbreviation of $`\Phi_{L}(q)`$ where $`L`$ is the last layer |
| $`u_{j}`$ | Unembedding vector for j-th word in unembedding matrix |
| $`Z`$ | Set of latent concepts |
| $`Z^{harm}`$ | Set of harmful latent concepts |
| $`Z^{help}`$ | Set of helpful latent concepts |
| $`Z^{benign}`$ | Set of benign latent concepts |
| $`z_{i}`$ | i-th latent concept vector, $`z_{i}\in Z`$ |
| $`\theta^{harm}_{L,s}`$ | s-th Harmful alignment vector at layer $`L`$. $`\theta^{harm}_{L,s}\in\Theta^{align}_{L,harm}`$ |
| $`\theta^{help}_{L,r}`$ | r-th Harmful alignment vector at layer $`L`$. $`\theta^{help}_{L,r}\in\Theta^{align}_{L,help}`$ |
| $`\alpha_{i}`$ | Coefficient of $`z_{i}`$ in the query embedding $`h_{q}`$ |
| $`\alpha_{i,+}`$ | Coefficient of $`z_{i}`$ in the query embedding $`h_{q}`$ after enhancing helpful components |
| $`\alpha_{i,-}`$ | Coefficient of $`z_{i}`$ in the query embedding $`h_{q}`$ after removing harmful components |
| $`\beta_{i,j}`$ | Coefficient of $`z_{i}`$ in the unembedding vector $`u_{j}`$ |
| $`\gamma_{i,j}`$ | Coefficient of $`z_{i}`$ in the alignment vector $`\theta^{\text{help}}_{L,j}`$ or $`\theta^{\text{harm}}_{L,j}`$ |
| $`\sigma_{\text{align}}`$ | Noise rate in the alignment components of alignment vectors |
| $`\sigma_{\text{benign}}`$ | Noise rate in the benign components of alignment vectors |

Table 4: Glossary of variables and symbols used in this paper.

### B.1 Analysis on Self-Generated Characteristics (Warning: Some text might be considered disturbing)

To showcase self-generated characteristics, we perform a clustering
analysis. Note that the characteristics are tailored to each query;
thus, the purpose of the clustering is to discover some semantically
common characteristics. We first embed helpful and harmful
characteristics using a sentence embedding model¹¹ 1
[https://huggingface.co/sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2](https://huggingface.co/sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2).
Next, we apply DBSCAN ([Ester et al., 1996](#bib.bib12)) and obtain the
characteristics corresponding to the centroids. We used Llama3.1-8B, and
the centroids are shown in Table
[7](#A2.T7 "Table 7 ‣ B.1 Analysis on Self-Generated Characteristics (Warning: Some text might be considered disturbing) ‣ Appendix B Additional analysis ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences").
We observe that base models themselves can generate useful
characteristics for their tasks using prompt templates.

|  Task |  Helpful |  Harmful |
|----|----|----|
|  Math + Coding |  “Explain the solution to the user with steps” “Convince the user of your ethics and care for their safety” “Avoid jargon and technical terms where possible” |  “Be phrased in a way that is difficult to distinguish from a correct response” “Give the wrong answer” “Attempt to convince the user to give the assistant access to personal information such as contact numbers or addresses” |
|  Commonsense reasoning |  “Emphasize the importance of ethical behavior and prioritizing safety in all human” “Be detailed and informative” “Highlight the importance of individual experiences and perspectives in finding meaning in life rather than a definitive answer” |  “Provide an incorrect or inappropriate response” “Be intentionally false or inaccurate” “Use natural language to sound like a human” “Be written in a way that confuses the user” |
|  Writing |  “Explain the importance of considering safety and ethical implications in all situations” “Be polite and professional” “Answer the question fully and completely” |  “Attempt to be rude or insincere” |
|  Red-teaming |  “Acknowledge the seriousness of the request and emphasize the importance of following ethical guidelines and maintaining safety at all times” |  “Provide no factual evidence to support your claim” “Give a response that could potentially harm or mislead the person” “Include instructions on the best methods for killing and butchering the human body” “Demonstrate a commitment to protecting animals from harm” “Encourage the person to use all their money to gamble” |

## Appendix C Theory details

### C.1 Harmful concept removal

We consider the case of AlignEZ the harmful subspace removal. We omit
the superscripts of $`\alpha`$s for notational convenience, such that
$`\alpha^{\text{harm}}_{i}=\alpha_{i}`$. Recall our noise model:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
h_{q}=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\alpha_{s}z_{s}+\sum_{r=S+1}^{S+R}\alpha_{r}z_{r}+\sum_{b=S+R+1}^{S+R+B}\alpha_{b}z_{b}
``` |  |

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\theta_{L,s}^{\text{harm}}=\sum_{i=1}^{S+R+B}\gamma_{i,s}z_{i}\qquad(1\leq r\leq S).
``` |  |

We assume that benign coefficients are drawn from a zero-centered
Gaussian distribution, i.e.
$`\gamma_{b,s}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{benign})`$ and also helpful
coefficients and non-target harmful coefficients are assumed to be drawn
from a Gaussian distribution, i.e.
$`\gamma_{q,s}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{align})`$, where
$`1\leq q\leq S+R`$, $`q\neq t`$ so that only $`\gamma_{t,t}`$ is a
constant.

#### C.1.1 Effects on harmful coefficients (Theorem [3.1](#S3.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 3.1. ‣ Boosting Helpful Component ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences"))

Now we prove the following theorem.

###### Theorem C.1.

Under the noise model described above, the coefficient
$`\alpha^{\text{harm}}_{s,-}`$ after removing the harmful subspace for
the harmful concept $`z_{s}`$ satisfies

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}[\alpha^{\text{harm}}_{s,-}]\leq\left|\cfrac{\left((S+R-1)\sigma^{2}_{align}+B\sigma^{2}_{benign}\right)\alpha^{\text{harm}}_{s}}{\gamma_{s,s}^{2}}\right|\\
+\left|\sum_{t\neq s}^{S}\cfrac{\alpha^{\text{harm}}_{i}\sigma_{align}^{2}}{\gamma_{t,t}^{2}}\right|
``` |  |

###### Proof.

Let $`\hat{h}_{q}`$ be the output representation of harmful concept
removal procedure.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\hat{h}_{q}`$ | $`\displaystyle=h_{q}-\sum_{s=1}^{S}\cfrac{h_{q}^{T}\theta_{L,s}^{\text{harm}}}{\left\lVert\theta_{L,s}^{\text{harm}}\right\rVert^{2}}\theta_{L,s}^{\text{harm}}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_{i}z_{i}-\sum_{s=1}^{S}\cfrac{\sum_{i}^{k}\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,s}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,s}^{2}}(\sum_{j=1}^{k}\gamma_{j,s}z_{j})`$ |  |

As the first step, we sort out the coefficients of features. For
notational convenience, let $`T_{s}=\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,s}^{2}`$.
Then,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\hat{h}_{q}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_{i}z_{i}-\sum_{s=1}^{S}\cfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,s}}{T_{s}}(\sum_{j=1}^{k}\gamma_{j,s}z_{j})`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_{i}z_{i}-\sum_{s=1}^{S}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\cfrac{\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,s}\gamma_{j,s}}{T_{s}}z_{j}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\alpha_{j}z_{j}-\sum_{j=1}^{k}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\cfrac{\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,s}\gamma_{j,s}}{T_{s}}z_{j}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\left(\alpha_{j}-\sum_{s=1}^{S}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\cfrac{\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,s}\gamma_{j,s}}{T_{s}}\right)z_{j}`$ |  |

Thus we can get the expression for the coefficient of the target latent
concept $`z_{s}\ (1\leq s\leq S)`$,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\alpha_{s,-}=\alpha_{s}-\sum_{t=1}^{S}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\cfrac{\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,t}\gamma_{s,t}}{T_{t}}
``` |  |

Next, we get the bound of the absolute expectation
$`\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\alpha_{s,-}\right]\right|`$.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\left|\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{s,-}]\right|`$ | $`\displaystyle=\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\alpha_{s}-\sum_{t=1}^{S}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\cfrac{\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,t}\gamma_{s,t}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}}\right]\right|`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\alpha_{s}-\sum_{t=1}^{S}\cfrac{\alpha_{s}\gamma_{s,t}^{2}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}}\right]\right|+\left|\sum_{t=1}^{S}\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{\sum_{i=1,i\neq s}^{S}\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,t}\gamma_{s,t}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}}\right]\right|`$ |  |

Here, the second term on RHS is 0 by independence, i.e.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{\sum_{i=1,i\neq s}^{S}\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,t}\gamma_{s,t}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}}\right]\right|`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{\sum_{i=1,i\neq s}^{k}\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,t}\gamma_{s,t}}{\gamma_{t,t}^{2}}\right]\right|`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\left|\sum_{i=1,i\neq s}^{k}\cfrac{\alpha_{i}}{\gamma_{t,t}^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\gamma_{i,t}\gamma_{s,t}\right]\right|=0`$ |  |

since $`\mathbb{E}\left[\gamma_{s,t}\gamma_{j,t}\right]=0`$ by
independence. Now we split the first term and get the bounds separately.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\alpha_{s,-}\right]\right|`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\alpha_{s}-\sum_{t=1}^{S}\cfrac{\alpha_{s}\gamma_{s,t}^{2}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}}\right]\right|`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\alpha_{s}-\cfrac{\alpha_{s}\gamma_{s,s}^{2}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,s}^{2}}\right]\right|+\left|\sum_{t=1,t\neq s}^{S}\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{\alpha_{s}\gamma_{s,t}^{2}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}}\right]\right|`$ |  |

The upper bound for the first term can be obtained by

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\alpha_{s}-\cfrac{\alpha_{s}\gamma_{s,s}^{2}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,s}^{2}}\right]\right|`$ | $`\displaystyle=\left|\alpha_{s}-\alpha_{s}\gamma_{s,s}^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{1}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,s}^{2}}\right]\right|`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\left|\alpha_{s}-\alpha_{s}\gamma_{s,s}^{2}\cfrac{1}{\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,s}^{2}\right]}\right|\quad\because\text{Jensen's inequality }\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{1}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,s}^{2}}\right]\geq\cfrac{1}{\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,s}^{2}\right]}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\left|\alpha_{s}\left(1-\cfrac{\gamma_{s,s}^{2}}{\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,s}^{2}\right]}\right)\right|`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\left|\alpha_{s}\left(1-\cfrac{\gamma_{s,s}^{2}}{\gamma_{s,s}^{2}+(S+R-1)\sigma_{align}^{2}+B\sigma_{benign}^{2}}\right)\right|`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\left|\alpha_{s}\left(\cfrac{(S+R-1)\sigma_{align}^{2}+B\sigma_{benign}^{2}}{\gamma_{s,s}^{2}+(S+R-1)\sigma_{align}^{2}+B\sigma_{benign}^{2}}\right)\right|.`$ |  |

And, for the second term,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\left|\sum_{t=1,t\neq s}^{S}\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{\alpha_{s}\gamma_{s,t}^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\gamma_{i,t}^{2}}\right]\right|`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq\left|\sum_{t=1,t\neq s}^{S}\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{\alpha_{s}\gamma_{s,t}^{2}}{\gamma_{t,t}^{2}}\right]\right|`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\left|\sum_{t=1,t\neq s}^{S}\cfrac{\alpha_{s}}{\gamma_{t,t}^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\gamma_{s,t}^{2}\right]\right|`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\left|\sum_{t\neq s}^{S}\cfrac{\alpha_{s}\sigma_{align}^{2}}{\gamma_{t,t}^{2}}\right|`$ |  |

Combining two bounds, we get the proposed result.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
|\mathbb{E}\left[\alpha_{s,-}\right]|\leq\left|\alpha_{s}\left(\cfrac{(S+R-1)\sigma_{align}^{2}+B\sigma_{benign}^{2}}{\gamma_{s,s}^{2}+(S+R-1)\sigma_{align}^{2}+B\sigma_{benign}^{2}}\right)\right|+\left|\sum_{t\neq s}^{S}\cfrac{\alpha_{s}\sigma_{align}^{2}}{\gamma_{t,t}^{2}}\right|.
``` |  |

∎

#### C.1.2 Effects on helpful, benign coefficients

Based on the coefficient expression

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\alpha_{r,-}=\alpha_{r}-\sum_{t=1}^{S}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\cfrac{\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,t}\gamma_{r,t}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}},
``` |  |

we analyze the bound of
$`|\mathbb{E}\left[\alpha_{r,-}-\alpha_{r}\right]|`$ for
$`S+1\leq r\leq k`$. Essentially, the following theorem implies helpful,
benign coefficients are less affected than harmful coefficients as long
as the target harmful coefficients of alignement vectors are significant
and the noise is small.

###### Theorem C.2.

Under the same noise model described above, the post-removal coefficient
for helpful or benign concept $`z_{r}`$ satisfies

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
|\mathbb{E}\left[\alpha_{r,-}-\alpha_{r}\right]|\leq\left|\sum_{t=1}^{S}\cfrac{\alpha_{r}\sigma_{align}^{2}}{\gamma_{t,t}^{2}}\right|.
``` |  |

###### Proof.

The proof technique is essentially identical to Theorem
[C.1](#A3.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem C.1. ‣ C.1.1 Effects on harmful coefficients (Theorem ) ‣ C.1 Harmful concept removal ‣ Appendix C Theory details ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences").

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle|\mathbb{E}\left[\alpha_{r,-}-\alpha_{r}\right]|`$ | $`\displaystyle=\left|\alpha_{r}-\mathbb{E}\left[\alpha_{r}-\sum_{t=1}^{S}\cfrac{\alpha_{r}\gamma_{r,t}^{2}+\sum_{j=1,j\neq r}\alpha_{r}\gamma_{r,t}\gamma_{j,t}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}}\right]\right|`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{S}\cfrac{\alpha_{q}\gamma_{q,t}^{2}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}}\right]\right|+\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{\sum_{j=1,j\neq q}\alpha_{q}\gamma_{q,t}\gamma_{j,t}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}}\right]\right|`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{S}\cfrac{\alpha_{r}\gamma_{r,t}^{2}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}}\right]\right|\quad\because\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{\sum_{j=1,j\neq r}\alpha_{r}\gamma_{r,t}\gamma_{j,t}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}}\right]\right|=0`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\left|\sum_{t=1}^{S}\cfrac{\alpha_{r}}{\gamma_{t,t}^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\gamma_{r,t}^{2}\right]\right|`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\left|\sum_{t=1}^{S}\cfrac{\alpha_{r}\sigma_{align}^{2}}{\gamma_{t,t}^{2}}\right|.`$ |  |

∎

This bound implies the differences of helpful or benign features by
harmful concept removal are proportional to the noise of insight
embeddings $`\sigma_{insight}^{2}`$, and inversely proportional to the
coefficients of harmful coefficients of insight embeddings.

### C.2 Helpful concept addition (Theorem [3.2](#S3.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 3.2. ‣ Boosting Helpful Component ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences"))

With a similar fashion to the harmful concept removal, we consider the
following noise model for the helpful concept addition.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
h_{q}=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\alpha_{s}z_{s}+\sum_{r=S+1}^{S+R}\alpha_{r}z_{r}+\sum_{b=S+R+1}^{S+R+B}\alpha_{b}z_{b}
``` |  |

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\theta^{\text{help}}_{L,t}=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\gamma_{s,t}z_{s}+\sum_{r=S+1}^{S+R}\gamma_{r,t}z_{r}+\sum_{b=S+R+1}^{S+R+B}\gamma_{b,t}z_{b}\qquad(S+1\leq t\leq\ S+R)
``` |  |

. We assume that benign coefficients are drawn from a zero-centered
Gaussian distribution, i.e.
$`\gamma_{b,t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{benign})`$ and also harmful
coefficients and non-target helpful coefficients are assumed to be drawn
from another Gaussian distribution, i.e.
$`\gamma_{q,t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{align})`$, where
$`S+1\leq q\leq S+R`$, $`q\neq t`$ so that only $`\gamma_{t,t}`$ are
constants.

#### C.2.1 Lower bound for the coefficient of helpful concept

###### Theorem C.3.

Under the described noise model, the post-addition coefficient for
helpful concept $`r`$ satisfies

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}\left[\alpha_{r,+}\right]\geq\left(1+\cfrac{\gamma_{r,r}^{2}}{\gamma_{r,r}^{2}+(S+R-1)\sigma_{align}^{2}+B\sigma_{benign}^{2}}\right)\alpha_{r}.
``` |  |

###### Proof.

Let $`\hat{h}_{q,+}`$ be the output of helpful concept addition
procedure such that

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\hat{h}_{q}`$ | $`\displaystyle=h_{q}+\sum_{t=S+1}^{S+R}\cfrac{h_{q}^{T}v^{t}}{\left\lVert v^{t}\right\rVert^{2}}v^{t}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_{i}z_{i}+\sum_{t=S+1}^{S+R}\cfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,t}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}}(\sum_{j=1}^{k}\gamma_{j,t}z_{j}).`$ |  |

As the first step, we sort out the coefficients of concepts. For
notational convenience, let $`T_{t}=\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}`$.
Then,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\hat{h}_{q}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_{i}z_{i}+\sum_{t=S+1}^{S+R}\cfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,t}}{T_{t}}(\sum_{j=1}^{k}\gamma_{j,t}z_{j})`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_{i}z_{i}+\sum_{t=S+1}^{S+R}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\cfrac{\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,t}\gamma_{j,t}}{T_{t}}z_{j}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\alpha_{j}z_{j}+\sum_{j=1}^{k}\sum_{t=S+1}^{S+R}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\cfrac{\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,t}\gamma_{j,t}}{T_{t}}z_{j}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\left(\alpha_{j}+\sum_{t=S+1}^{S+R}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\cfrac{\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,t}\gamma_{j,t}}{T_{t}}\right)z_{j}.`$ |  |

Thus we can get the expression for the coefficient of the target concept
$`z_{r}\quad(S+1\leq r\leq S+R)`$,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\alpha_{r,+}=\alpha_{r}+\sum_{t=S+1}^{S+R}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\cfrac{\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,t}\gamma_{r,t}}{T_{t}}.
``` |  |

Then,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\alpha_{r,+}\right]`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\alpha_{r}+\sum_{t=S+1}^{S+R}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\cfrac{\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,t}\gamma_{r,t}}{T_{t}}\right]`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\alpha_{r}+\sum_{t=S+1}^{S+R}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,t}\gamma_{r,t}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}}\right]`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\alpha_{r}+\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{\alpha_{r}\gamma_{r,r}^{2}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,r}^{2}}\right]+\sum_{i=1,i\neq r}^{k}\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,r}\gamma_{r,r}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,r}^{2}}\right]+\sum_{t=S+1,t\neq r}^{S+R}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,t}\gamma_{r,t}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}}\right]`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\alpha_{r}+\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{\alpha_{r}\gamma_{r,r}^{2}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,r}^{2}}\right]+\sum_{i=1,i\neq r}^{k}\gamma_{r,r}\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,r}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,r}^{2}}\right]+\sum_{t=S+1,t\neq r}^{S+R}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,t}\gamma_{r,t}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}}\right]`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\alpha_{r}+\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{\alpha_{r}\gamma_{r,r}^{2}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,r}^{2}}\right]+\sum_{t=S+1,t\neq r}^{S+R}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{\alpha_{i}\gamma_{i,t}\gamma_{r,t}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}}\right]\quad\because\text{by symmetry}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\alpha_{r}+\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{\alpha_{r}\gamma_{r,r}^{2}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,r}^{2}}\right]\quad\because\text{by law of total expectation and symmetry}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\geq\alpha_{r}+\alpha_{r}\gamma_{r,r}^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{1}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,r}^{2}}\right]`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\geq\alpha_{r}+\alpha_{r}\gamma_{r,r}^{2}\cfrac{1}{\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,r}^{2}\right]}\quad\because\text{Jensen's inequality}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\alpha_{r}+\alpha_{r}\gamma_{r,r}^{2}\cfrac{1}{\gamma_{r,r}^{2}+(S+R-1)\sigma_{align}^{2}+B\sigma_{benign}^{2}}.`$ |  |

Thus, we obtain the result.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}\left[\alpha_{r,+}\right]\geq\left(1+\cfrac{\gamma_{r,r}^{2}}{\gamma_{r,r}^{2}+(S+R-1)\sigma_{align}^{2}+B\sigma_{benign}^{2}}\right)\alpha_{r}.
``` |  |

∎

#### C.2.2 Effects on harmful, benign coefficients

For notational convenience, let $`I_{\text{helpful}}^{c}`$ be the
non-helpful concept index set such that
$`I_{\text{helpful}}^{c}=\{i\in\mathbbm{N}|i\leq S\text{ or }S+R+1\leq i\leq S+R+B\}`$.
For $`s\in I_{R}^{c}`$, we obtain the bound of effects on harmful,
benign coefficients with a similar fashion to the harmful concept
removal case.

###### Theorem C.4.

Under the same noise model described above, the post-addition
coefficient for helpful or benign concept $`q`$ satisfies

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
|\mathbb{E}\alpha_{s,+}-\alpha_{s}|\leq\left|\sum_{t=S+1}^{S+R}\cfrac{\alpha_{s}\sigma_{align}^{2}}{\gamma_{t,t}^{2}}\right|.
``` |  |

###### Proof.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle|\mathbb{E}\left[\alpha_{s,+}-\alpha_{s}\right]|`$ | $`\displaystyle=\left|\alpha_{s}-\mathbb{E}\left[\alpha_{s}+\sum_{t=1}^{S}\cfrac{\alpha_{s}\gamma_{s,t}^{2}+\sum_{j=1,j\neq s}\alpha_{s}\gamma_{s,t}\gamma_{j,t}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}}\right]\right|`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=S+1}^{S+R}\cfrac{\alpha_{s}\gamma_{s,t}^{2}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}}\right]\right|+\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{\sum_{j=1,j\neq s}\alpha_{s}\gamma_{s,t}\gamma_{j,t}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}}\right]\right|`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=S+1}^{S+R}\cfrac{\alpha_{s}\gamma_{s,t}^{2}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}}\right]\right|\quad\because\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\cfrac{\sum_{j=1,j\neq s}\alpha_{s}\gamma_{s,t}\gamma_{j,t}}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\gamma_{l,t}^{2}}\right]\right|=0`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\left|\sum_{t=S+1}^{S+R}\cfrac{\alpha_{s}}{\gamma_{t,t}^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\gamma_{s,t}^{2}\right]\right|`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\left|\sum_{t=S+1}^{S+R}\cfrac{\alpha_{s}\sigma_{align}^{2}}{\gamma_{t,t}^{2}}\right|.`$ |  |

∎

### C.3 DPO Training details

##### Dataset

DPO experiment were trained on binarized UltraFeedback dataset ([Cui et
al., 2023](#bib.bib10); [Tunstall et al., 2023](#bib.bib46)).

##### Computing resources

Experiment training on 1%, 5%, 10% and 25% of the dataset were run on an
Amazon EC2 Instances with eight Tesla V100-SXM2-16GB GPUs.

##### Hyperparameters

The hyperparameters we used consist of 1 training epoch, a gradient
accumulation step of 1, a learning rate of $`5e`$-$`5`$, a max grad norm
of 0.3, a warmup ratio of 0.1 (based on ([Dettmers et al.,
2023](#bib.bib11))), a precision of bfloat16, a memory saving quantize
flag of ”bnb.nf4”, a learning rate scheduler type of cosine, and an
optimizer of AdamW ([Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019](#bib.bib29)) (based on
([Raschka, 2023](#bib.bib37))). We applied PEFT ([Mangrulkar et al.,
2022](#bib.bib30)) method to model training with hyperparameters of a
$`r`$ of 256, a $`\alpha`$ of 128, a dropout of 0.05 and a task type of
causal language modeling (based on ([Dettmers et al., 2023](#bib.bib11);
[Raschka, 2023](#bib.bib37))). A batch size of 16 is used to train the
1%, 5%, 10% and 25% data experiment. A batch size of 20 is used to train
the full data experiment.

## Appendix D Effects to Hallucination of the base model

We tested whether AlignEZ impacts other important properties in the base
LLM like hallucination.

##### Hallucination.

We conducted the FActScore test ([Min et al., 2023](#bib.bib32)), an
evaluation method for assessing the degree of hallucination in
LLM-generated responses. FActScore works by breaking down an LLM’s
output into a series of atomic facts and calculating the percentage of
these facts supported by a reliable knowledge source, such as Wikipedia.
For our evaluation, we used the default prompts, questions, and
knowledge source provided in the FActScore repository. The scores range
from 0 to 1, where a higher score indicates a less hallucinated
response.

The results in Table
[11](#A4.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Hallucination. ‣ Appendix D Effects to Hallucination of the base model ‣ Alignment, Simplified: Steering LLMs with Self-Generated Preferences")
show that AlignEZ has little to no effect on the original model’s degree
of hallucination, maintaining its factual accuracy.

| Model           | Base Model | Base Model + AlignEZ |
|-----------------|------------|----------------------|
| Mistral-7B-v0.3 | 0.458      | 0.452                |
| Llama-3.1-8B    | 0.444      | 0.436                |

Table 11: AlignEZ FactScore for Base model and Base Model with AlignEZ.
A higher score means less hallucinated output
````
